docs.title: Flexiv TDK Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the Flexiv TDK (Teleoperation Development Kit) documentation site. This site provides a user manual, API reference, and Q&A to help you integrate and operate Flexiv's teleoperation SDK.

This source tree is TDK v1.6.4. The C++ library is a self-contained shared object whose only public dependency is flexiv_rdk 1.9.4.1. The Python package requires flexivrdk==1.9.4.1. The hosted GitHub Pages site is TDK v2.x; preview these pages locally with mkdocs serve.

docs.title: What is Flexiv TDK?
docs.text: Flexiv TDK is an SDK for building custom robot-to-robot or device-to-robot teleoperation applications with Flexiv's adaptive robots. It enables synchronized, force-guided motion using high-fidelity perceptual feedback and supports both LAN (Local Area Network) and WAN (Internet) connections.

docs.title: Contact-Rich Manipulation Benchmarks
docs.text:
Flexiv TDK has been recognized on the Manipulation Net Peg-in-Hole Leaderboard. The Manipulation Net is a public benchmark for robotic manipulation in the real world at scale with any robot at any time and anywhere. This provides external evidence for the contact-rich manipulation capability relevant to TDK use cases, including compliant insertion, alignment, and force-sensitive teleoperation workflows.

🎬 Flexiv's TDK | Teleoperation Made Simple (Click image below to play)

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• High Fidelity Perceptual Feedback: 100% tactile feedback transparency ensures the fidelity of human operation.
  • Better Physical Human-Robot Interaction: The leader robot can be repositioned or reoriented at any time. Upon re-engagement, only relative motion is mapped—no absolute pose constraints.
  • Selective Cartesian Constraints: Constrain motion along specific directions for faster, more precise task execution.
  • Robust Force/Moment Protection: Prevents damage to the robot and workpiece while ensuring intrinsic safety during contact.
  • LAN/WAN Support: Flexible network configurations for both LAN and WAN.

docs.title: Q: Which platforms are supported?
docs.text:
A: Ubuntu 22.04+ on x86_64 and aarch64 (C++ and Python 3.10/3.12/3.14). macOS 14+ on arm64 (C++ and Python 3.10/3.12). Toolchain: GCC ≥ 11 (Linux) or Apple Clang ≥ 15 (macOS), CMake ≥ 3.16.3.

TDK C++ RDK Python RDK v1.6.4 (flexivtdk==1.6.4) flexiv_rdk 1.9.4.1 flexivrdk==1.9.4.1

pip install flexivtdk==1.6.4 installs flexivrdk==1.9.4.1 automatically. Do not mix TDK 1.6.4 with another flexivrdk version.

docs.title: Q: Do I need a real-time kernel?
docs.text: A: Not strictly, but a low-latency or RT kernel improves responsiveness and stability for teleoperation. See Real-Time Kernel.

docs.title: Q: How do I sync time for WAN teleoperation?
docs.text: A: Use Chrony to sync system clocks on both ends. See Time Sync (WAN).

docs.title: Q: Where is the API reference?
docs.text: A: The online GitHub Pages site is TDK v2.x. For this v1.6.x tree, generate Doxygen locally (doxygen docs/doxygen/Doxyfile.in) and serve the site with mkdocs serve. See the repository README.

docs.title: Q: What if my app cannot find shared libraries?
docs.text: A: Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib (Linux) or DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib (macOS) before running binaries.

docs.title: Q: Where can I get help?
docs.text: A: Open an issue on GitHub or contact Flexiv via https://www.flexiv.com/contact.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The repository includes example applications for both C++ and Python.

This release uses NetworkCfgStd for WAN Standard Edition TCP peer-to-peer. The WAN -W / --wan-iface argument is an OS interface name (for example wlo1 or enp3s0), not an IPv4 address. -A / --lan-ip remains the LAN IPv4 address of the NIC connected to the robot.

Console commands added in v1.6.4:

  • h: print GetTeleopStatus() (why teleop is restricted or paused, and what to do next)
  • WAN n: print role() and robot_pair_sn()
  • LAN H: HomeAll()
  • quit (LAN and WAN transparent examples): stop teleop and exit the program

docs.title: WAN Professional Edition example
docs.text:
transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan_pro (C++ and Python) uses NetworkCfgPro instead of TCP peer-to-peer. Both sides connect through a TDK Server deployment.

  • -c <client.conf>: path to client.conf from the TDK Server credential package (required).
  • -n <gripper_name>: optional. Name of the follower gripper configured in Elements -> Device. When provided, the example also creates a GripperRemoteControl instance. Both leader and follower must pass the same name. The follower enables the gripper locally at startup; the leader controls it with the console commands G/D/N (enable, disable, init), o/c/s (open, close, stop), and t/P (print states and params).
  • -D: optional, leader only. DI0 engages arm teleop. With -n, a rising edge on DI1 toggles the follower gripper between open and closed, and the console gripper motion commands o/c/s are disabled.

docs.title: C++ Examples
docs.text:
Location: example/

Examples include: - transparent_cartesian_teleop_lan.cpp - transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan.cpp - transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan_pro.cpp - joint_teleop_under_lan.cpp

Build and run:

cd flexiv_tdk/example
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=~/tdk_install
cmake --build . --config Release -j 4
./<program_name> [arguments]

If the loader cannot find libflexiv_tdk / libflexiv_rdk:

# Linux
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib ./<program_name> [arguments]

# macOS
DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib ./<program_name> [arguments]

docs.title: Python Examples
docs.text:
Location: example_py/

Examples include: - transparent_cartesian_teleop_lan.py - transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan.py - transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan_pro.py - joint_teleop_under_lan.py

Install TDK v1.6.4 first. It requires flexivrdk==1.9.4.1 (pulled in automatically):

python3.x -m pip install flexivtdk==1.6.4

Some console commands in examples (for example LAN P, which calls instances()) use the underlying RDK Robot objects and need that matching flexivrdk package.

Run:

cd flexiv_tdk/example_py
python3.x <example_name>.py [arguments]

Replace 3.x with your Python version.

docs.title: User Manual Overview
docs.text:
This manual guides you through installing, configuring, and using the Flexiv TDK (Teleoperation Development Kit) to build teleoperation applications over LAN or WAN.

This documentation source is TDK v1.6.4. Version mapping for this release:

TDK C++ RDK Python RDK v1.6.4 (flexivtdk==1.6.4) flexiv_rdk 1.9.4.1 (only public C++ dependency) flexivrdk==1.9.4.1

The online GitHub Pages site documents TDK v2.x and must not be used with this release. Generate this manual locally (see the repository README).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text:
• Application developers integrating teleoperation features
  • Robotics engineers deploying Flexiv systems
  • Researchers building custom haptic or robot-to-robot workflows

docs.title: Robot
docs.text: • At least two Flexiv Rizon robots with FT sensors configured

docs.title: Network Devices
docs.text:
• Network devices (e.g., Ethernet switch/router) with sufficient bandwidth and latency
  • CAT 6 or CAT 7 Ethernet cables

docs.title: User PC
docs.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04+ (x86_64 or aarch64): C++ and Python 3.10/3.12/3.14
  • macOS 14+ (arm64): C++ and Python 3.10/3.12
  • C++ toolchain: GCC ≥ 11 (Linux) or Apple Clang ≥ 15 (macOS), CMake ≥ 3.16.3
  • Network access to the robot and (for WAN) reliable time synchronization

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
• include/: C++ headers
  • example/: C++ example apps
  • example_py/: Python example apps
  • docs/doxygen/: Doxygen configuration and assets

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
• New to the SDK? Start with Quick Start (Python) or Quick Start (C++).
  • Need hard real-time performance? See Real-Time Kernel.
  • Deploying over WAN? See Time Sync (WAN).
  • Looking for sample usage? See Examples.
  • Third-party licenses for the prebuilt library: see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the repository.

docs.title: Quick Start (C++)
docs.text:
This guide covers building and using Flexiv TDK as a CMake package.

Version mapping: TDK v1.6.4 is a self-contained shared library. The only public C++ dependency is flexiv_rdk 1.9.4.1. Third-party libraries are embedded and hidden. thirdparty/build_and_install_dependencies.sh installs RDK.

docs.title: 1) Install build dependencies
docs.text:
# Linux
sudo apt install build-essential cmake cmake-qt-gui -y

# macOS (Xcode command-line tools + Homebrew CMake)
xcode-select --install
brew install cmake

docs.title: 2) Choose an install directory
docs.text:
Example:

mkdir -p ~/tdk_install

docs.title: 3) Build and install third-party dependencies
docs.text:
cd flexiv_tdk/thirdparty
bash build_and_install_dependencies.sh ~/tdk_install

Internet access to GitHub is required.

docs.title: 4) Configure and install TDK
docs.text:
cd flexiv_tdk
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=~/tdk_install
cmake --build . --target install --config Release

docs.title: 5) Link TDK in your project
docs.text:
cd flexiv_tdk/example
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=~/tdk_install
cmake --build . --config Release -j 4

docs.title: 6) Run examples
docs.text:
CMake records the install lib directory in the example's rpath, so Linux and macOS can run the binary directly:

cd flexiv_tdk/example/build
./<program_name> [arguments]

TDK looks up libflexiv_rdk next to itself ($ORIGIN / @loader_path). The install lib directory must contain both libraries (.so on Linux, .dylib on macOS). Fallback:

# Linux
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib ./<program_name> [arguments]

# macOS
DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib ./<program_name> [arguments]

See Examples for details on the example programs.

docs.title: Quick Start (Python)
docs.text:
This guide walks you through installing and running the Flexiv TDK Python package.

Version mapping: TDK v1.6.4 (flexivtdk==1.6.4) requires RDK v1.9.4.1 (flexivrdk==1.9.4.1). Do not mix this TDK release with another flexivrdk version.

docs.title: 1) Install the package
docs.text:
python3.x -m pip install flexivtdk==1.6.4

flexivtdk==1.6.4 declares a hard dependency on flexivrdk==1.9.4.1, so pip installs that RDK wheel automatically.

Replace 3.x with your Python version. Linux supports 3.10, 3.12, and 3.14; macOS supports 3.10 and 3.12.

docs.title: 2) Verify installation
docs.text:
python3.x
>>> import flexivtdk
>>> flexivtdk.__version__
>>> import flexivrdk
>>> flexivrdk.__version__

Confirm flexivtdk is 1.6.4 and flexivrdk is 1.9.4.1.

docs.title: 3) Run Python examples from this repo
docs.text:
cd flexiv_tdk/example_py
python3.x <example_name>.py [arguments]

Check each example’s source code for usage details.

docs.title: Common Tips
docs.text:
• Ensure the robot network connection is stable.
  • For WAN teleop, see Time Sync (WAN).
  • For real-time performance, see Real-Time Kernel.

docs.title: Real-Time Kernel Options
docs.text: Not all use cases require a real-time OS, please read below to determine if you need it.

docs.title: ⚙️ Kernel Options for Real-Time Performance
docs.text:
Ubuntu offers multiple kernel variants tailored for different workloads:

Kernel Type Description Typical Use Case generic Default kernel: balanced performance & power management General desktop/server use lowlatency Reduced interrupt latency; better scheduling responsiveness Robotics, audio processing, soft real-time rt (PREEMPT_RT) Fully preemptible; hard real-time determinism Industrial control, mission-critical systems

docs.title: ⚠️ Important Disclaimer
docs.text:
Upgrading to a low-latency or real-time (RT) kernel may: - Break proprietary drivers (e.g., NVIDIA, Wi-Fi modules) - Cause system instability or boot failure

You assume full responsibility for any issues arising from kernel changes. ✅ Always back up your system before proceeding.

docs.title: Install Low-Latency or PREEMPT_RT Kernel for Ubuntu/x84-64
Option 1: Low-Latency Kernel
docs.text:
1. Install the kernel: For Hardware Enablement (HWE) stack (check with uname -r; e.g., Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel 6.x), use:

bash sudo apt update && sudo apt install --install-recommends linux-lowlatency-hwe-22.04 # replace "22.04" with your version For the original kernel (5.15), use: bash sudo apt update && sudo apt install --install-recommends linux-lowlatency

  1. Set GRUB to prefer low-latency: bash echo 'GRUB_FLAVOUR_ORDER="lowlatency"' | sudo tee -a /etc/default/grub sudo update-grub

  2. Reboot and verify: bash sudo reboot uname -r # Should show "...-lowlatency"

🔄 To revert to generic, change GRUB_FLAVOUR_ORDER="generic" and run sudo update-grub.

docs.title: Option 2: PREEMPT_RT Kernel
docs.text:
Ubuntu releases listed in this page have native real-time kernel support, and can be easily enabled via a few commands, see full tutorial at https://ubuntu.com/real-time.

ℹ️ Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 users can enable RT kernel via free Ubuntu Pro subscription. The subscription is free for personal use.

ℹ️ For Nvidia Jetson(arrch64), please refer to Nvidia's official documentation.

docs.title: Robots setup and network configuration
docs.text: Before using TDK, ensure that the robots are properly mounted and the network is correctly configured. TDK supports both local area network (LAN) and wide area network (WAN) deployments. The following section uses a LAN setup as an example to describe the network configuration for the robots and the user computer.

docs.title: ⚠️ Important
docs.text: Please make sure all robots are well mounted on a fixed base and are powered on before proceeding to the next step.

docs.title: Step 1: Power on and servo on the robots
docs.text: Follow instructions in the provided Quick Start Guide to complete hardware setup and boot up the two robots. After booting up, connect the robots to the UI tablet (Flexiv Elements). All the light rings on the robots should be deep blue if they are powered on and servo on.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable Remote Mode - Ethernet
docs.text:
Go to Settings > Remote Mode on the Flexiv Elements. To enable Remote Mode, turn on the toggle, then select Ethernet from the Select a Mode drop-down list

View the currently applied Ethernet communication protocol(s). If no license has been installed, you can install the TDK license in Settings > License.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the network for leader robot and follower robot
docs.text:
The network configuration for the leader robot and follower robot can be done via the Flexiv Elements->Settings->Network. Please refer to Flexiv Elements User Manual for more details.

For LAN teleoperation, please set both robots and the user's computer to the same network segment with different IP Addresses (e.g., leader robot: 192.168.2.110, follower robot: 192.168.2.111 and user PC:192.168.2.112. All configured with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0).

docs.title: Step 4: Reboot the robots and ping test
docs.text: After configuring the network and remote mode, reboot the robots. Connect the user's computer and two robots to the same ethernet switch. Ping the two control boxes to make sure all the devices are connected properly.

docs.title: WAN (Standard Edition)
docs.text:
WAN teleoperation uses NetworkCfgStd (TCP peer-to-peer). There is one robot and one edge computer on each side. One edge computer is the TCP server and the other is the TCP client. Either side may be the server.

The TCP client only needs Internet access. The TCP server also needs:

  1. NAT enabled on the router that the server edge computer is connected to (usually on by default).
  2. The private IPv4 address of the server edge computer, used for a TCP port-forwarding rule. The forwarded port is listening_port on both sides.
  3. The server's public IPv4 address (for example from https://whatismyipaddress.com/). Both sides must set the same public_ipv4_address.

Example flags (see transparent_cartesian_teleop_wan):

  • -t server|client: TCP role
  • -i <public_ip>: public IPv4 of the TCP server
  • -p <port>: forwarded listening port (same on both sides)
  • -A <lan_ipv4>: optional LAN IPv4 of the NIC connected to the robot
  • -W <iface>: optional WAN interface name (for example wlo1 or enp3s0), not an IPv4 address. Repeatable.

Both sides of a pair must use the same public IPv4 and listening port. Synchronize the two edge computers' clocks before running WAN teleop; see Time Sync (WAN).

docs.title: Time Sync (WAN)
docs.text: Accurate time synchronization is critical for WAN teleoperation. When operating over the internet, each edge computer must have its system time calibrated.

docs.title: 1) Install and start Chrony
docs.text:
sudo apt install chrony -y
systemctl status chrony  # should show "active (running)"

docs.title: 2) Check sync accuracy
docs.text:
chronyc tracking | grep 'System time\|RMS offset'
Metric Good (ms) Acceptable (ms) Poor (ms) System time < 1 1 - 10 > 10 RMS offset < 5 5 - 20 > 20

docs.title: 3) Force immediate sync (if needed)
docs.text:
sudo chronyc burst 4/4
sudo chronyc makestep

After network changes (e.g., Wi-Fi → Ethernet), restart:

sudo systemctl restart chronyd
sleep 5
sudo chronyc makestep

Learn more: chrony

docs.title: Build Issues
docs.text:
• CMake cannot find Flexiv TDK: Ensure -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=~/tdk_install points to the install prefix.
  • Missing dependencies: Re-run thirdparty/build_and_install_dependencies.sh and ensure the install directory exists.

docs.title: Runtime Issues
docs.text:
• Shared library not found: Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH=~/tdk_install/lib before running binaries.
  • Permission issues with real-time priorities: Add your user to /etc/security/limits.conf for rtprio and nice.

docs.title: WAN Teleoperation
docs.text:
• High latency / unstable motion: Verify network stability and re-check time synchronization.
  • Time sync inaccurate: Use chronyc tracking and consider re-running chronyc burst and chronyc makestep.
